title: Cooking Techniques Glossary
description: Core culinary techniques used across world cuisines, grouped by category.

techniques.name: Roasting
techniques.description: Cooking food uncovered with hot, dry air, typically in an oven, producing browned exteriors via the Maillard reaction.

techniques.name: Grilling
techniques.description: Cooking directly over a heat source (charcoal, gas, or wood), giving food a charred exterior and smoky flavour.

techniques.name: Sautéing
techniques.description: Cooking quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, keeping food moving in the pan.

techniques.name: Stir-frying
techniques.description: A Chinese technique of tossing small, uniformly cut pieces of food in a wok over very high heat for a very short time, prized for producing 'wok hei' (the smoky flavour from the seared, high-heat surface of the wok).

techniques.name: Deep-frying
techniques.description: Fully submerging food in hot oil, producing a crisp exterior through rapid moisture evaporation.

techniques.name: Baking
techniques.description: Cooking with dry, enclosed heat, typically used for breads, pastries, and casseroles.

techniques.name: Braising
techniques.description: Searing food first, then slow-cooking it partially submerged in liquid in a covered pot — combines dry- and moist-heat cooking to tenderise tougher cuts.

techniques.name: Steaming
techniques.description: Cooking food with the vapour from boiling water, without direct contact with the liquid, preserving moisture and nutrients.

techniques.name: Poaching
techniques.description: Gently cooking food fully submerged in liquid kept just below a simmer, ideal for delicate items like eggs and fish.

techniques.name: Simmering
techniques.description: Cooking food in liquid held just below boiling point, used for stocks, soups, and stews.

techniques.name: Blanching
techniques.description: Briefly boiling food, then plunging it into ice water to halt cooking — used to set colour, loosen skins, or partially cook before freezing.

techniques.name: Sous-vide
techniques.description: Vacuum-sealing food and cooking it in a precisely temperature-controlled water bath for extended periods, a technique that emerged from French and industrial food-science research in the 1970s-1980s and later spread into fine dining.

techniques.name: Fermentation
techniques.description: Using bacteria, yeast, or mould to transform food, developing flavour and preserving it — one of humanity's oldest food technologies.

techniques.name: Curing
techniques.description: Preserving food (usually meat or fish) with salt, sugar, nitrates, or a combination, often followed by drying or smoking.

techniques.name: Smoking
techniques.description: Exposing food to smoke from smouldering wood, both flavouring and preserving it.

techniques.name: Pickling
techniques.description: Preserving food in an acidic liquid (vinegar) or through fermentation in brine, extending shelf life while adding tang.

techniques.name: Canning
techniques.description: Sealing food in airtight containers and heat-treating it to destroy spoilage organisms — developed by Nicolas Appert in France in 1809-1810.

techniques.name: Nixtamalization
techniques.description: Soaking and cooking corn in an alkaline solution (traditionally limewater), an ancient Mesoamerican technique that improves nutrition and makes corn grindable into masa.

techniques.name: Marinating
techniques.description: Soaking food (usually meat) in a seasoned liquid before cooking to add flavour and, with acidic or enzymatic marinades, tenderise it.

techniques.name: Tempering spices (tadka/tarka)
techniques.description: Briefly frying whole spices in hot oil or ghee to release their aromatic oils before adding them to a dish — foundational to Indian cooking.

techniques.name: Emulsifying
techniques.description: Combining two liquids that don't normally mix (like oil and water) into a stable blend, usually with an emulsifier like egg yolk or mustard.

techniques.name: Reduction
techniques.description: Simmering a liquid uncovered to evaporate water and concentrate flavour and thicken texture.

techniques.name: Laminating dough
techniques.description: Repeatedly folding butter or fat into dough to create many thin alternating layers, which puff apart during baking.

techniques.name: Kneading
techniques.description: Working dough by hand or machine to develop gluten strands, giving bread its structure and chew.

techniques.name: Whisking
techniques.description: Rapidly beating ingredients to incorporate air or combine them smoothly, used for everything from egg whites to sauces.

techniques.name: Deglazing
techniques.description: Adding liquid (wine, stock, or water) to a hot pan to lift the browned, flavourful bits (fond) left after searing, forming the base of a pan sauce.

techniques.name: Basting
techniques.description: Spooning or brushing fat or pan juices over food as it cooks to keep it moist and add flavour to the surface.

techniques.name: Proofing
techniques.description: Letting yeasted dough rest in a warm place so the yeast produces gas and the dough rises before baking.

techniques.name: Julienne
techniques.description: Cutting vegetables into long, thin matchstick strips, roughly 1/8 inch (3 mm) square and a few inches long.

techniques.name: Brunoise
techniques.description: A fine dice made by first julienning, then cutting across into tiny 1/8 inch (3 mm) cubes -- one of the smallest classic knife cuts.

techniques.name: Batonnet
techniques.description: A thicker matchstick cut, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) square, often the starting point for a small dice.

techniques.name: Dicing
techniques.description: Cutting food into cubes, classically graded small, medium, or large depending on the size needed.

techniques.name: Mincing
techniques.description: Chopping food (especially garlic and herbs) into very small, irregular pieces, finer than a dice.

techniques.name: Chiffonade
techniques.description: Stacking and rolling leafy herbs or greens, then slicing across into thin ribbons.

techniques.name: Rondelle
techniques.description: Slicing a cylindrical vegetable straight across into round discs.

techniques.name: Paysanne
techniques.description: Thin, flat cuts of vegetables into small squares or triangles, traditionally used in rustic soups.

techniques.name: Tourné
techniques.description: A classic French technique for hand-carving a vegetable into a small, seven-sided, football-like shape with rounded ends.

techniques.name: Chopping
techniques.description: A rougher, less precise cut than dicing, used when uniform size matters less than speed.

techniques.name: Filleting
techniques.description: Using a flexible, sharp knife to separate fish flesh from its bones and skin in clean sheets.

techniques.name: Supreme (citrus segmenting)
techniques.description: Cutting away the peel and pith of a citrus fruit, then slicing between the membranes to release clean, membrane-free segments.
